learning_outcomes: Distinguish market demand from quantity demanded, and market supply from quantity supplied
Label and draw a demand curve and a supply curve with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis
Find and interpret equilibrium price and quantity from schedules, a diagram or simple linear relationships
Identify whether a scenario changes a curve position or causes movement along an unchanged curve
Show supply and demand shifts separately, then compare the original and new equilibria
Explain the business consequences of market shifts while stating the assumptions and limits of the model

teaching_content.core_explanation: A market price is influenced by both what buyers are prepared to purchase and what sellers are prepared to provide. A demand schedule shows quantities buyers would purchase at a range of prices, assuming other relevant circumstances do not change. A supply schedule shows quantities sellers would offer at those prices under the same assumption. A graph can plot both relationships with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. Their intersection is the modelled equilibrium: the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. If the price is above it, planned supply can exceed demand; below it, planned demand can exceed supply. These pressures indicate a possible adjustment, not a guarantee that real markets immediately clear.
definitions: Market demand: quantities all buyers plan to purchase at different possible prices, under stated conditions
Quantity demanded: units purchasers plan to buy at one particular price
Market supply: quantities sellers plan to offer at different possible prices, under stated conditions
Quantity supplied: units offered at one particular price
Equilibrium: a modelled price and quantity at which planned purchases and sales match
Curve shift: a change in planned demand or supply at each given price due to a determinant other than the product's own price
Movement along a curve: a change in quantity demanded or supplied when the product's own price changes and other determinants are held fixed
mechanisms: A rise in suppliers' input costs can make fewer units economical to supply at any particular selling price, shifting market supply left
A subsidy that lowers producers' costs can shift market supply right; an indirect tax borne by suppliers can shift supply left, depending on pass-through and other conditions
An increase in preference for a product can shift demand right; an increase in the price of a substitute may also increase this product's demand
A supply-left shift, with demand unchanged, tends to raise the modelled equilibrium price and lower traded quantity
A demand-right shift, with supply unchanged, tends to raise both modelled price and traded quantity
A price change caused by the shift of one curve leads to movement along the other curve, not an automatic shift of it

misconceptions.incorrect: A higher selling price shifts the market demand curve left.
misconceptions.correction: Changing a product's own price moves the quantity demanded along its existing demand curve; an independent demand determinant shifts the curve.

misconceptions.incorrect: A rise in the cost of production shifts the supply curve right.
misconceptions.correction: Holding other circumstances fixed, increased unit costs tend to lower quantity supplied at each given price, shifting supply left.

misconceptions.incorrect: When supply falls, the higher resulting price shifts demand to the left too.
misconceptions.correction: With demand determinants unchanged, the price response is movement along the same demand curve.

misconceptions.incorrect: Any price above equilibrium instantly causes the market to return to equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: The diagram predicts incentives for adjustment; contractual, capacity, regulatory and information frictions can delay or prevent it.

misconceptions.incorrect: The same shock affects every market by the same amount.
misconceptions.correction: The magnitude depends on curve shapes, sensitivity, timing, market boundaries and simultaneous influences.

boundaries: The downward demand/upward supply model is a simplified ceteris paribus depiction, not a universal curve shape
A firm’s operational capacity is related to but not equivalent to an entire market supply schedule
Supply and demand changes occurring together can leave the direction of price or quantity indeterminate without further information
An equilibrium point is a model of planned quantities rather than a promise about real-time transactions
Elasticity measures responsiveness; it is related to but not interchangeable with drawing a shift or computing equilibrium

original_numeric_case.context: A hypothetical local market for refill packs. Each quantity represents packs offered or requested per week. Coefficients are teaching simplifications, not real consumer estimates.
demonstration_steps: Identify quantities as functions of price, and label P and Q on the correct axes.
Set the baseline demand and supply quantities equal: 120 - 4P = 20 + P. Solve to get P=20 and Q=40.
For higher production costs replace S0 with S1: 120 - 4P = 10 + P. P=22; then Q=32. Keep D0 in the diagram.
For stronger customer preference instead replace D0 with D1: 130 - 4P = 20 + P. P=22; then Q=42. Keep S0 in the diagram.
Compare P and Q against the baseline and explain the different market mechanism for each scenario.
Distinguish the curve that shifts from movement along the unchanged curve; discuss real-world limitations before applying to a business decision.
